topics.title: The world through a bird's eyes

learn.hook: Ever wondered what your school looks like to a kite flying overhead? Let's borrow a bird's wings!
points: 'What a Bird Thought' is a poem about how a bird sees and thinks about the world around it.
In a poem, the speaker may be an animal or a thing, not a person. Here the speaker is a bird.
A 'bird's-eye view' means a view from high above, where big things look small.
Poets use images (word pictures) so we can see what the speaker sees.
To understand a poem, read it twice, picture each line, and ask: Who is speaking? What do they see? How do they feel?

example.q: Read this original poem: From high above, the town looks small, / The cars are scattered painted toys; / The river is a silver thread, / The bus, a beetle, makes no noise. / I wonder if the people know / How tiny all their worries seem / When seen from up among the clouds, / Where every road is like a dream. Who is the speaker and what do they notice?
steps: 'From high above' and 'among the clouds' show the speaker is flying — a bird.
The bird sees cars like toys, the river like a thread, the bus like a beetle.
It also wonders whether people know how small their worries look from above.
example.answer: A bird flying high; it notices that everything below looks tiny, and so do people's worries.

learn.reallife: Photos taken by drones or from aeroplane windows give us a bird's-eye view of fields, rivers and cities.

games.title: About the bird poem
items: The speaker of the poem is a bird.
It looks down 'from high above' and 'among the clouds'.
The bus looks huge to the bird.
The bus looks like a small beetle.
The river looks like a silver thread.
Line 3 says so.
The bird thinks people's worries look tiny from above.
Lines 5-6 say their worries seem tiny.
'toys' and 'noise' are rhyming words.
Both end with the same '-oise/-oys' sound.

quiz.q: In the bird poem, the river is called "a silver thread". Why?
options: The river is made of silver
From high above, a shining river looks long and thin
quiz.explain: From the sky a river looks thin and shiny, like a silver thread.

quiz.q: In the poem, "The bus, a beetle, makes no noise." Why does the bus make no noise for the bird?
options: The bird is too high to hear it
The bus is made of paper
quiz.explain: From far up in the sky, the bird cannot hear the bus.

quiz.q: From where is the bird looking at the town?
options: from high above, among the clouds
quiz.explain: Lines 1 and 7 say 'from high above' and 'among the clouds'.
quiz.mistake: Does not use the place clues in the poem

quiz.q: What does the bird wonder about?
options: Whether people know how tiny their worries seem from above
quiz.explain: Lines 5-6: 'I wonder if the people know how tiny all their worries seem.'
quiz.mistake: Picks an image instead of the bird's thought

quiz.q: What is a 'bird's-eye view'?
options: A close look at a bird's eye
A view from under the ground
quiz.explain: It is an idiom meaning a view from a great height.

quiz.q: Which word rhymes with 'seem' in the poem?
quiz.explain: 'Seem' and 'dream' share the '-eam' sound.
quiz.mistake: Chooses a word that looks similar but doesn't rhyme

quiz.q: What is the mood of the bird poem?
quiz.explain: The bird gently wonders about the world below — a calm, thoughtful mood.
quiz.mistake: Does not read the tone of the words

quiz.q: Why do the cars look like toys to the bird?
options: Things look smaller from far away
The bird is a toy collector
The cars are painted by children
quiz.explain: Distance makes big objects look small.

teach.ask: Gappu flies high: 'Everything looks tiny from up here! Why does the poem say the river is a silver thread?'
teach.praise: Tweet! From high up, a river looks thin and shiny like a silver thread. Poets paint with words!
teach.nudge: Why do things look smaller when you see them from the sky?

topics.title: Seeing from another point of view

learn.hook: To an ant, a puddle is an ocean. To you, it's just a puddle. Who is right? Both!
points: Perspective (point of view) is the way someone sees or thinks about something. It depends on where they are and what they know.
The same event can look different to different people: rain is a joy for a farmer but a problem for a cricket match.
First-person writing uses 'I', 'me', 'we' (the narrator is in the story). Third-person writing uses 'he', 'she', 'they' (the narrator is outside the story).
Changing the point of view can change how a story feels. Imagine your school day told by your school bag!
Seeing other perspectives helps us understand people better and avoid quick judgements.

example.q: Think it through: Rewrite in the first person, as if the bird is speaking: 'The bird looked down and saw the town.'
steps: The narrator becomes the bird itself.
Keep the rest of the sentence.
example.answer: I looked down and saw the town.

learn.reallife: In a cricket match, a 'no-ball' may look different to the batter, the bowler and the umpire — that's why we have replays!

games.title: First or third person?
items: I flew over the river.
We built a nest together.
My wings felt tired.
She flew over the river.
They built a nest together.
His wings felt tired.

quiz.q: What does 'perspective' mean?
options: the way someone sees or thinks about something
quiz.explain: Perspective means point of view.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of the word

quiz.q: Which sentence is written in the first person?
options: She saw the river from the sky.
They saw the river from the sky.
I saw the river from the sky.
The bird saw the river from the sky.
quiz.explain: First person uses 'I' or 'we'.

quiz.q: Which sentence is in the third person?
options: My friend and I climbed the neem tree.
quiz.explain: Third person uses he, she, it or they.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any sentence about someone else is first person

quiz.q: To a tiny ant, a puddle may look like:
quiz.explain: From the ant's tiny point of view, a puddle is enormous.
quiz.mistake: Sees only from a human point of view

quiz.q: Rain stops a school sports day. Who is most likely to see the rain as good news?
options: a runner who trained for the race
a child who wanted to win a medal
a farmer whose crops need water
quiz.explain: Crops need water, so a farmer welcomes rain.
quiz.mistake: Does not think about other people's needs

quiz.q: Why is it useful to see things from another person's perspective?
options: It makes us forget our own ideas
It helps us win every argument
It helps us understand people and avoid quick judgements
It is only useful in maths
quiz.explain: Understanding others' points of view makes us fairer and kinder.

quiz.q: Change to the first person: 'The parrot ate a green chilli.'
quiz.explain: In the first person, the parrot would say 'I'.

quiz.q: The poem tells what the bird sees using 'I'. So it is told from the bird's:
quiz.explain: The poem gives the bird's own point of view.
quiz.mistake: Does not link 'I' with the speaker's point of view

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'My friend the ant says the puddle is an ocean. I say it's a puddle. Who's right?'
teach.praise: Chirp! We're both right — it depends on perspective. Different eyes see things differently!
teach.nudge: Why might the ant and I see the same puddle differently?

learn.hook: 'The bus is like a beetle' and 'The bus is a beetle' — one little word makes all the difference!
points: A simile compares two different things using 'like' or 'as': 'The cars look like toys', 'as light as a feather'.
A metaphor compares by saying one thing IS another, without 'like' or 'as': 'The river is a silver thread.'
Both help readers picture something clearly and in a fresh way.
Common similes: as busy as a bee, as brave as a lion, as cool as a cucumber, as white as snow, as slow as a snail.
Tip: look for 'like' or 'as ... as' to spot a simile; if one thing is simply called another, it is a metaphor.

example.q: Think it through: Is this a simile or a metaphor? 'Grandma's lap is a soft pillow.'
steps: Look for 'like' or 'as' — there isn't one.
It says the lap IS a pillow.

learn.reallife: Cricket commentators love them: 'He's a wall at the crease!' (metaphor) or 'The ball flew like a rocket!' (simile).

games.title: Simile or metaphor?
items: The cars look like toys.
She is as brave as a lion.
He runs like the wind.
The river is a silver thread.
My brother is a couch potato.
The classroom was a zoo.

quiz.q: Which sentence contains a simile?
options: The moon is a silver plate.
The moon shone like a silver plate.
quiz.explain: It compares the moon to a plate using 'like'.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every description is a simile

quiz.q: Which sentence contains a metaphor?
options: The river is like a silver thread.
The river is as shiny as silver.
The river is a silver thread.
quiz.explain: It says the river IS a thread, without 'like' or 'as'.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a simile with a metaphor

quiz.q: Complete the simile: 'as brave as a ___'
quiz.explain: 'As brave as a lion' is a common simile.

quiz.q: Which words help us spot a simile?
quiz.explain: Similes compare using 'like' or 'as'.

quiz.q: 'My little sister is a chatterbox.' This is a metaphor that means she:
quiz.explain: Calling her a chatterbox means she chatters (talks) a lot.

quiz.q: 'As cool as a cucumber' describes someone who is:
quiz.explain: This simile means calm and relaxed, even under pressure.

quiz.q: Which is a simile?
options: Her smile was as bright as the sun.
quiz.explain: It compares a smile to the sun using 'as ... as'.

quiz.q: In the bird poem, "Where every road is like a dream" uses:
quiz.explain: It compares roads to a dream using 'like', so it is a simile.

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: 'Simile, metaphor, simile, metaphor... they both compare things. What's the difference?'
teach.praise: Tweet! A simile uses like or as; a metaphor just says it IS the thing. I'm as happy as a lark!
teach.nudge: Which one uses the words 'like' or 'as'?
